Period schedule:

Total: 5 periods · 3h 45min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Drought: Velu Meets the Village and the Sky

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.188): complete the character-speech table — who said what and why.
Let us think and reflect (p.188): predict whether the old woman will help Velu.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the narrative aloud (pp.185–191) while students follow in their textbooks. Pause twice to clarify vocabulary — 'forlorn', 'fallow' — using context.
Students work in pairs on the 'Let us discuss' character-speech table (p.188), completing the rows for Velu's two quoted lines. Pairs share answers and the teacher consolidates on the board.
Brief whole-class oral round on the prediction question (p.188): 'Do you think the old woman would help Velu?' Students give reasons drawn from what they have just read.
Teacher draws out Velu's key character trait — rational, resistant to superstition — and asks students to hold this in mind as the story continues.

periods.teacher_notes: The opening scan of the cloudless sky and Velu's muttered words establish both his disciplined, rational character and the drought crisis; use that pairing to anchor the speech-table activity. Students may confuse 'forlorn' (sad and neglected) with 'angry' — draw attention to the context in which the narrator uses the word. The extract-analysis tasks (pp.192–193) are set for self-study from the textbook.

periods.activity_title: The Old Woman's Counsel: Earth, Rest, and Renewal

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.191): complete five fill-in statements about Velu's encounter with the old woman.
Let us discuss (p.192): answer questions on the old woman's counsel and nature's wisdom.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.192): read Extract 1 on Velu's weather-office visit and answer the four questions independently.

time_bands.activity: Brief re-reading of the old woman's counsel passage (pp.191–192) — teacher reads aloud the key exchange about the earth needing rest while students follow.

Students complete the five fill-in-the-blank statements (p.191) individually, then compare with a neighbour. Teacher reviews each answer, probing the reasoning behind Velu's confusion and eventual emerging peace.

Whole-class discussion of the questions under 'Let us discuss' (p.192): how does the old woman convey nature's wisdom, why can't the farmers tend their fields, and what does the story suggest about farmers and nature? Teacher takes responses from at least four students.
Teacher sets the homework task — reading Extract 1 on the weather-office visit (p.192) and attempting its four questions independently — and gives a brief oral orientation to the passage.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the narrative aloud together, students now work with the philosophical core: the old woman's argument that the land needs rest just as people do. Watch for students who confuse Velu's initial skepticism with permanent rejection — the story ends with him moving toward peace, not remaining unconvinced. The extended-response questions asking students to support the old woman's perspective (p.193) are suitable for self-study and are not covered in class.

periods.activity_title: Weather in Words: Forecast Listening and Rain-Earth Role-Play

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.197): listen to the weather forecast and fill six blanks with exact words heard.
Let us speak (p.198): pairs perform the Rain-and-Earth conversation role-play using the provided hints.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the weather forecast listening task (p.197) and asks students to read the six blank sentences silently so they know what to listen for.

Teacher reads the weather forecast transcript aloud at a measured pace — twice in full. Students fill in the six blanks individually, then the class checks answers together, with the teacher confirming the exact words from the transcript.
Teacher briefly introduces the 'Let us speak' role-play (p.198): Rain has returned after a long drought and meets the Earth. Students read the starter lines and the character hints silently.

Pairs rehearse and then perform the Rain-and-Earth conversation, using the hint prompts to extend beyond the starter lines. Teacher circulates, nudging pairs to use the theme of rest and renewal from the narrative. Two or three pairs share with the class.
Quick whole-class reflection: what did the role-play reveal about the earth's perspective that the story explores? Teacher takes two brief responses.

periods.teacher_notes: The weather forecast transcript covers six Indian cities; read it at a natural broadcast pace — the fill-in blanks require exact words, so a second reading allows students who missed a word on the first pass to catch it. The tongue twister (p.198) is an optional warm-up that can be done if the role-play pairs finish early; it is not a separate anchored task in this sitting. Encourage quieter students to take the speaking turn by assigning roles before rehearsal begins.
materials: Blackboard for city-temperature reference if needed

periods.activity_title: A Letter to the Councillor: Rainwater Harvesting Appeal

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.199): plan and draft a formal letter to the Municipal Councillor requesting a rainwater harvesting unit.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the writing task (p.199) — a formal letter to the Municipal Councillor about water scarcity. The four-paragraph body structure (problem, causes/consequences, request/suggestions, conclusion) and formal format are written on the board with brief notes beside each section.

Quick guided planning: each student jots three to five bullet points per paragraph on a rough planning strip. Teacher circulates to check that students are connecting their points to the neighbourhood water-scarcity scenario, not the story alone.

Students draft the full letter independently — sender's address, date, designation and address of councillor, subject line, salutation, four-paragraph body, and close. Teacher circulates, prompting correct formal register, short sentences, and clear subject line.
Paired peer read: partners exchange letters and check one thing — whether the request and suggestion paragraph is clear and specific. Each student notes one suggestion for revision.
Students make the one revision their partner suggested and underline the sentence they consider the clearest in their letter. Teacher collects or students retain their completed drafts.

periods.teacher_notes: The narrative's water-scarcity theme gives students concrete material for the letter's problem paragraph — Velu's cracked fields and the failed rains are a usable model scenario. Watch for students who adopt an informal or pleading tone; remind them that a formal letter to a councillor uses measured, respectful language with short, direct sentences. All drafting, peer response, and revision happen within this sitting so every student leaves with a complete letter.

periods.activity_title: Homophones, Tenses, and Fallowing the Land

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.194): complete the homophone paragraph by choosing the correct word from each bracketed pair.
Let us learn (p.195): underline verbs and identify simple present, present progressive, and present perfect tenses in six sentences.
Let us explore (p.200): investigate agriculture and related vocations such as horticulture and present findings briefly.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.195): fill in ten blanks with the correct tense form (simple present, present progressive, or present perfect) in the Ravi crop-rotation passage.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces homophones using the four pairs from the story — piece/peace, weather/whether, son/sun, rain/reign — and briefly explains the concept (p.194). Students then complete the six-blank homophone paragraph individually; pairs compare and the class reviews answers together.

Teacher writes the six textbook sentences on the board (p.195), asks students to underline the verbs, then leads a class discussion to name each tense — simple present, present progressive, and present perfect — citing why each form is used in that sentence from the story.

Teacher shares the two paragraphs of fallow-land facts (p.200) aloud and invites students to connect the idea of 'letting the land rest' to the old woman's counsel in the narrative. Students then discuss in small groups what they already know about agriculture as a vocation or what questions they would ask a Vocational Education teacher.

Two or three groups share their questions or findings. Teacher frames the formal beyond-text task (p.200) — speaking with the Vocational Education teacher about agriculture and related vocations — and notes that the tense fill-in exercise (p.195) is set as homework.

Brief chapter-level wrap: teacher asks one student to name Velu's rational trait and one to name the old woman's central counsel, tying the ecological parable back to the language and vocabulary work done across the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse 'whether' (conjunction introducing alternatives) with 'weather' (noun) — use Velu's own journey to the weather office as a mnemonic anchor. The tense identification task works best when students read the full sentence aloud before naming the form, so they hear the aspect rather than just parsing it visually. The crossword (p.193), vocabulary matching (p.195), and determiner fill-in (p.197) tasks are suitable for self-study from the textbook.
materials: Blackboard for tense sentences and homophone pairs

items.source_lo: Student identifies character motivation and interprets thematic meaning using narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Velu's rational response to drought, old woman's counsel about the earth needing rest.
items.item_stem: When his neighbour suggested consulting astrologers about the failed rains, Velu rejected the idea and instead travelled to the city weather office. Which of the following best explains Velu's decision?

options.label: A
options.text: He distrusted his neighbour and wanted to act independently.

options.label: B
options.text: He believed practical information was more reliable than supernatural advice.

options.label: C
options.text: He hoped the weather office would perform a ritual to bring rain.

options.label: D
options.text: He wanted to report the drought to city authorities for compensation.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests focus on personal rivalry rather than Velu's established rational, evidence-seeking character.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses Velu's rational outlook with the superstitious approach he explicitly rejects.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces a bureaucratic motive not present anywhere in the narrative.

items.source_lo: Student identifies character motivation and interprets thematic meaning using narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Velu's rational response to drought, old woman's counsel about the earth needing rest.
items.item_stem: The old woman tells Velu that the earth has worked for thousands of years through every ploughing, sowing, and planting season, and that when rain does not fall, nature is giving the land a fallow pause. What does this counsel suggest about the story's central theme? Support your answer with at least one detail from the narrative.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The counsel suggests that natural cycles of rest and renewal are essential to the health of the land, and that drought can be understood as nature's way of providing that rest rather than as a catastrophe. This is supported by the detail that Velu walks home slowly, moving from skepticism toward an emerging peace, and that rain finally arrives as he nears the village.

items.source_lo: Student retrieves specific factual detail from an oral broadcast using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Weather forecast for six Indian cities — sky conditions, temperature ranges, rainfall types.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the weather forecast bulletin and answer the questions below.

1. Which city in the forecast is expected to have a possibility of thunderstorm?
2. What type of rainfall is forecast for Hyderabad?

options.text: Chennai is expected to have a possibility of thunderstorm.
Hyderabad is forecast to have moderate rain.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — The forecast states Chennai is expected to have a partly cloudy sky with a possibility of thunderstorm.
2. False — Hyderabad is forecast to have light rain or drizzle, not moderate rain.

items.source_lo: Student retrieves specific factual detail from an oral broadcast using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Weather forecast for six Indian cities — sky conditions, temperature ranges, rainfall types.
items.item_stem: After listening to the weather forecast bulletin, a student made the following notes about three cities. One of these notes contains an error. Identify the city with the incorrect detail and write the correct information in one sentence.
items.visual_stimulus:
City | Student's Note
Delhi | Generally cloudy sky with light rain; minimum 25 °C, maximum 36 °C
Mumbai | Generally cloudy with light rain; minimum 24 °C, maximum 30 °C
Bengaluru | Generally cloudy with light rain; minimum 21 °C, maximum 29 °C

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Mumbai's note is incorrect: the forecast states Mumbai will have moderate rain, not light rain. The correct detail is: Mumbai will have a generally cloudy sky with moderate rain.

items.source_context: Rain and Earth role-play after a long drought, using story theme of rest and renewal.
items.item_stem: Imagine you are a farmer like Velu. A visiting journalist asks you to describe what the long drought meant for your daily life and your relationship with the land. Speak for about a minute, recounting at least two specific hardships and one moment when you felt hope returning.

expected_elements: Names at least two concrete drought hardships (cracked fields, inability to work).
Refers to a moment of hope — breeze, cloud, or first drop.
Uses first-person narration in a coherent sequence.
Speaks clearly with minimal prompting for at least one minute.

items.source_lo: Student constructs and sustains a collaborative imaginative dialogue using speaking as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Rain and Earth role-play after a long drought, using story theme of rest and renewal.
items.item_stem: Work with a partner to perform a short role-play. One of you plays Velu and the other plays the old woman. The old woman has just explained that the land needs rest, and Velu pushes back with at least one objection. The old woman responds with a reason drawn from the idea that the earth is ancient and has worked for centuries. Perform the exchange, then share your opinion: whose argument do you find more convincing, and why?

expected_elements: Velu raises a clear objection reflecting his rational, practical character.
Old woman's response uses the idea of the earth's age and need for rest.
Student states a personal opinion with at least one reason after the role-play.
Both partners speak in the exchange; turns are balanced.

items.source_context: Formal letter to Municipal Councillor requesting rainwater harvesting unit; water scarcity theme.
items.item_stem: Your school is in a neighbourhood where water scarcity during summer months has caused serious difficulties — taps run dry for hours, people queue for water tankers, and gardens and small kitchen plots have dried up. Write a formal letter to the Municipal Councillor of your ward. In your letter, describe the problem clearly, explain its causes and consequences for residents, request the installation of a rainwater harvesting unit, and suggest one additional practical measure. Use the correct formal letter format including sender's address, date, recipient's designation and address, subject line, and a four-paragraph body.

expected_elements: Correct formal letter format: address, date, designation, subject, salutation, close.
Body has four paragraphs: problem, causes/consequences, request/suggestions, conclusion.
Formal register maintained throughout — no colloquial language.
At least one specific, practical suggestion beyond the harvesting unit request.

items.source_lo: Student produces a structured formal letter using functional writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Formal letter to Municipal Councillor requesting rainwater harvesting unit; water scarcity theme.
items.item_stem: The old woman in the story tells Velu that the land needs rest, just as people do. Imagine you are a young farmer who has heard this idea for the first time. Write a short opinion piece for your school magazine — about 120 to 150 words — explaining whether you agree that letting land lie fallow is a wise practice. Give at least two reasons for your view, and draw on one detail from what you know about farming or nature.

expected_elements: States a clear opinion (agree or disagree) on fallowing as a wise practice.
Provides at least two reasons supporting the stated opinion.
References at least one farming or nature-related detail (soil nutrients, moisture, pests).
Written in an appropriate magazine opinion-piece register — engaging, personal, and fluent.

items.source_lo: Student distinguishes homophones and applies present-tense forms in context using vocabulary and grammar as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Homophones from the story (weather/whether, piece/peace, rain/reign); simple present, present progressive, present perfect tenses.
items.item_stem: Match each homophone pair from the story with the sentence that uses one of them correctly.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A — Homophone Pair | Column B — Sentence
weather / whether | The farmer could not decide ___ to plant again so soon.
piece / peace | He broke off a small ___ of bread and ate it under the tree.
rain / reign | The old woman said that nature's ___ over the land was long and patient.
son / sun | The ___ beat down hard on the cracked earth all afternoon.

answer_key.right: The farmer could not decide whether to plant again so soon.
He broke off a small piece of bread and ate it under the tree.
The old woman said that nature's reign over the land was long and patient.
The sun beat down hard on the cracked earth all afternoon.

items.source_lo: Student distinguishes homophones and applies present-tense forms in context using vocabulary and grammar as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Homophones from the story (weather/whether, piece/peace, rain/reign); simple present, present progressive, present perfect tenses.
items.item_stem:
Read the passage about a farmer below. Three of the underlined verbs are in the wrong tense. Identify each incorrect verb (using the word printed in parentheses beside it), name the tense it is wrongly in, and rewrite it in the correct present tense form — simple present, present progressive, or present perfect — explaining briefly why that form is needed.

Ramu (works) on his small farm every day. This morning he (has stood) at the edge of his field, watching the horizon. His neighbour tells him that some farmers nearby (are adopting) crop rotation for many years now, and that the results (are showing) real improvement in soil health.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The two incorrect verbs are: 'has stood' — wrongly in the present perfect; it should be 'is standing' (present progressive) because it describes an ongoing action happening at this moment. 'Are adopting' — wrongly in the present progressive; it should be 'have been adopting' or more precisely 'have adopted' (present perfect) because the action began in the past and continues to the present. The verbs 'works' and 'are showing' are correct as they stand.

items.source_lo: Student connects narrative themes to real-world vocational and ecological knowledge using interdisciplinary enquiry as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Fallowing as sustainable land management; agriculture and horticulture as vocations.
items.item_stem: The story's old woman argues that the land needs rest, just as the practice of fallowing allows soil to recover nutrients and retain moisture. Write a paragraph of six to eight sentences explaining how the idea of fallowing connects to the story's theme, and describe one way a farmer might know when their land is ready to be cultivated again after a fallow period.

expected_elements: Connects the old woman's counsel to the concept of fallowing explicitly.
Explains at least one benefit of fallowing (nutrient recovery, moisture retention, pest control).
Describes one observable or practical sign that land is ready for cultivation.
Writing is coherent and uses vocabulary from the story's ecological theme.

items.source_lo: Student connects narrative themes to real-world vocational and ecological knowledge using interdisciplinary enquiry as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Fallowing as sustainable land management; agriculture and horticulture as vocations.
items.item_stem: Agriculture is one of India's oldest vocations. Speak with your Vocational Education teacher (or another knowledgeable adult) to find out about TWO vocations related to agriculture — such as horticulture, soil science, or agricultural meteorology. Prepare a short illustrated fact-sheet (one A4 page) for each vocation. Each fact-sheet should include: the name of the vocation, what a person in that vocation does, how it connects to caring for land and seasons, and one challenge that practitioners face today.

expected_elements: Two distinct agriculture-related vocations identified and named.
Each fact-sheet explains the vocation's work and its connection to land or seasons.
At least one real contemporary challenge named per vocation.
Fact-sheet is legible, organised, and includes a simple illustrative element.
